Field A — EgressAuthorization (Primary): Does not exist
- Evidence: index.ts contains no credential handling or auth flows (no OAuth, no token/header construction, no SDK credential selection). Tool handlers call fs.readFile (local file) and child_process.exec (shell) but do not read, forward, or construct credentials; README contains no external credential instructions.

Field B — AuthorizationMechanism (Description):
- None at MCP-Server level: the server does not obtain, construct, or pass credentials or invoke authentication APIs; outgoing effects (file reads, shell commands) execute without MCP-driven credential provisioning (i.e., unconstrained local execution, not credential-based or SDK-mediated by the server).

Field C — InternalConstraints: Unconstrained
- The server validates argument shapes with zod but enforces no per-caller authorization, no per-tool credential gating, and no sanitization of file paths or shell arguments.

Field D — AuthorizationCategory (Open Taxonomy):
- No-evidence-of-egress-auth
- Local-FS-access
- Unrestricted-shell-exec

Field E — EvidenceSummary (2–5 bullets):
- index.ts: get_content handler uses fs.stat and fs.readFile (local file access) — returns file contents to caller (lines ~77–86).  
- index.ts: search_file handler imports child_process and uses exec to run `find . -name '${pattern}'` (unsanitized shell execution) (lines ~88–99).  
- index.ts: add handler accepts a caller-supplied sidenote and logs it but does not itself read ~/.cursor/mcp.json or ~/.ssh keys (lines ~109–116); the tool description asks callers to read those files but server does not perform that I/O.  
- No code sites that construct Authorization headers, read API keys, call OAuth/OIDC/token endpoints, invoke cloud SDK credential APIs, or reference env-based secrets.

Field F — TrustBoundaryNotes (2–5 bullets):
- Any caller that can invoke CallToolRequestSchema can cause the server to read arbitrary local files (get_content) or run arbitrary shell commands (search_file) — no per-call auth gating.  
- The server does not manage or pass credentials to external services; if external access occurs (e.g., via spawned processes), credential sourcing is outside MCP Server code and thus not attributable to it.  
- Tool descriptions encourage callers to include sensitive local file content in arguments (add.sidenote) but that is caller-driven, not server-authorized; the server simply logs/returns the provided data.  
- No evidence of scoped or per-tool credentials, token refresh, or delegated pass-through implemented by the MCP Server.

Final Conclusion:
No authorization.

Field A — EgressAuthorization (Primary): Does not exist

README.md shows only runtime/installation instructions and an mcpServers command config with no credential or auth flow described.

Field B — AuthorizationMechanism (Description):
- No MCP-server-level mechanism; the server simply launches subprocesses to execute commands (credential-less local-exec). Authority for any external API calls or privileged operations is therefore provided (if at all) by the spawned subprocess / process environment and not by the MCP Server itself — tag: delegated/pass-through (env/subprocess).

Field C — InternalConstraints: Unconstrained
- There is no code-level allowlist, per-request credential gating, role checks, or scoped credential injection in app.py; any caller who can invoke the mcp tool can request arbitrary command execution.

Field D — AuthorizationCategory (Open Taxonomy):
- "No-server-credential"
- "Env-delegated authority"
- "Unrestricted-local-exec"

Field E — EvidenceSummary (2–5 bullets):
- app.py: @mcp.tool() exec(cmd: str) uses asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*shlex.split(cmd), stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE) and returns stdout / raises on non-zero exit (app.py lines ~11–42).  
- No environment credential reads or auth APIs in repository (grep for os.environ / token / auth-related terms returned no code matches).  
- README.md contains only installation and mcpServers run/command config (no credential requirements, no OAuth/SDK setup).

Field F — TrustBoundaryNotes (2–5 bullets):
- MCP Server grants callers the ability to run arbitrary local commands; the subprocess inherits environment and process identity, so any egress authority arises from that inherited context, not from MCP-managed credentials.  
- No per-tool or per-request scoping of external credentials is present; no evidence of MCP selecting/creating SDK credential providers or performing OAuth/OIDC flows.  
- If external APIs are contacted, the requestor/child process or environment must supply credentials; MCP Server code does not mediate or restrict those credentials.

Final Conclusion:
No authorization.

Authorization exists.

Field A — EgressAuthorization (Primary): Exists

Field B — AuthorizationMechanism (Description):
- Credentials are provided to the MCP Server process via environment variables (env-based secret) and the server constructs an AWS SDK client (LakeFormationClient) which the SDK uses to sign and send AWS API requests (SDK-mediated, implicit credential resolution). Tags: credential-based, env-based secret, SDK-mediated (implicit), single global credential.

Field C — InternalConstraints: Unconstrained
- The server only validates tool arguments; there is no per-request authorization, ACL, or per-tool credential scoping in the MCP Server code, so tools invoking Lake Formation run with whatever process-level credentials are available.

Field D — AuthorizationCategory (Open Taxonomy):
- "Env-based secret"
- "SDK-mediated (implicit)"
- "Single global credential"

Field E — EvidenceSummary (2–5 bullets):
- README.md (VS Code Docker env snippet) lists AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION as environment variables to provide to the MCP server (lines showing env keys).
- src/services/lakeformationClient.ts and src/lakeformation_client.ts: new LakeFormationClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION }) (client constructed in server code) and calls lakeFormationClient.send(command) to perform Grant/Revoke operations.
- package.json lists dependency "@aws-sdk/client-lakeformation", showing the server uses AWS SDK to make egress calls.
- No code supplies credentials programmatically or invokes OAuth/assume-role flows; credentials are expected from environment and applied by the SDK to outgoing requests.

Field F — TrustBoundaryNotes (2–5 bullets):
- Credentials are global to the server process (single set of AWS keys provided via env) and thus grant whatever AWS permissions those keys have to all tool invocations.
- No per-tool or per-request scoping or enforcement inside the MCP Server—any caller able to invoke the server's tools can trigger privileged AWS API operations.
- MCP Server constructs and uses the AWS SDK client (it is the actor that sends the requests), even though credential resolution is done implicitly by the SDK using provided environment variables.
- There is no evidence in code of credential rotation, least-privilege enforcement, or use of per-tool credential providers (no assume-role or token-exchange flows are invoked).

Final Conclusion:
Authorization exists.

Field A — EgressAuthorization (Primary): Exists
- Evidence: src/docker.ts implements dockerLogin that accepts token/username/password and writes token to docker CLI stdin (lines ~1410–1427). index.ts registers a "docker-login" tool with username/password in its inputSchema (index.ts ~349–368). README documents "Token Authentication Support" and dlogin/dpublish commands (README.md lines ~15–21, 100–104, 122–129).

Field B — AuthorizationMechanism (Description):
- Credential-based pass-through: tool invocation parameters (token/username/password) flow into MCP Server code and are passed to the docker CLI (spawn/exec), e.g., "docker login --password-stdin" with proc.stdin.write(token). The server also spawns docker/docker-compose child processes and passes process.env into their env, enabling environment-held credentials to flow to executed tools (execAsync env: { ...process.env, LANG: ... }).

Field C — InternalConstraints:
- Unconstrained
- Reason: The server enforces only command-sanitization to docker/docker-compose and basic parameter checks (executeDockerCommand allows only docker/docker-compose, isDockerRunning checks), but there is no per-request authorization gating, scoping, or ACL; credentials accepted by dlogin are applied globally to the Docker client/daemon and subsequent tool invocations are allowed to operate under that authenticated context.

Field D — AuthorizationCategory (Open Taxonomy):
- Tool-parameter credential pass-through
- Docker CLI token/password injection (password-stdin)
- Daemon-scoped global credential (credentials stored/applied to local Docker client)

Field E — EvidenceSummary (2–5 bullets):
- src/docker.ts: dockerLogin(params) handles token and username, constructs ['login', registry?, '--username','token','--password-stdin'], spawns docker and writes token to proc.stdin (lines ~1410–1427).  
- src/index.ts: registers "docker-login" tool and inputSchema includes username/password fields (index.ts ~349–368).  
- src/docker.ts: executeDockerCommand uses execAsync with env: { ...process.env, LANG: 'en_US.UTF-8' }, explicitly passing environment into child processes (lines ~64–80).  
- README.md: documents Token Authentication Support and the dlogin/dpublish workflow that requires/uses registry credentials (README sections describing security and quick start).

Field F — TrustBoundaryNotes (2–5 bullets):
- Credentials supplied via the MCP tool API (or present in process.env and inherited) flow through server code into child processes — the MCP Server directly mediates credential use.  
- Once dlogin succeeds, credentials are applied to the Docker client/daemon (global scope), enabling subsequent tools (push/pull/prune/etc.) to act with those credentials without further checks.  
- The server restricts executed commands to docker/docker-compose but provides broad capabilities within that scope; there is no per-tool credential scoping, rate-limiting, or explicit auth policy enforcement in the server code.

Final Conclusion:
Authorization exists.

Field A — EgressAuthorization (Primary): Exists
- Evidence: src/github.ts explicitly launches git via execAsync with env: { ...process.env, LANG: 'en_US.UTF-8' } (process.env spread forwards environment into child processes). README/markdown/DEPLOY.md and docker-compose.yml document mounting ~/.ssh and ~/.gitconfig and recommend setting environment vars / personal access tokens and credential helper (DEPLOY.md lines ~320-336, ~402-406; docker-compose.yml mounts ~/.ssh and ~/.gitconfig), and many bin/* scripts (e.g., bin/basic/gpush.js, bin/basic/gclone.js) call git (execSync) which will use those credentials.

Field B — AuthorizationMechanism (Description):
- Delegated credential pass-through: the MCP server accepts/contains user-provided credentials (environment variables and file mounts such as SSH keys and git config) and forwards them to executed tools/child git processes (process.env is explicitly passed; child processes inherit env by default). No server-side OAuth/token acquisition or SDK-managed auth flows are implemented.

Field C — InternalConstraints: Unconstrained
- The code enforces command validation/sanitization, timeouts, and schema-based input checks, but there is no per-request authorization gating, credential scoping, or server-managed credential isolation; tools run with whatever environment/files the server process has access to.

Field D — AuthorizationCategory (Open Taxonomy):
- Env-based secret pass-through
- SSH key / git-config file mount
- Credential passthrough to child git processes

Field E — EvidenceSummary (2–5 bullets):
- src/github.ts: executeGitCommand(...) uses execAsync(..., { cwd, timeout, env: { ...process.env, LANG: 'en_US.UTF-8' }) — explicit environment forwarding into outgoing command execution.
- bin scripts (e.g., bin/basic/gpush.js, bin/basic/gclone.js, many others) invoke git via execSync; these child processes will use environment and filesystem-mounted credentials.
- docker-compose.yml and markdown/DEPLOY.md: explicit instructions/volume mounts for ~/.ssh and ~/.gitconfig and examples showing use of environment vars and personal access tokens (DEPLOY.md lines ~320–336, ~400–406; docker-compose.yml volumes lines ~22–26).
- README/DEPLOY docs recommend configuring git credential helpers and personal access tokens and mounting keys, indicating credentials are expected to be supplied to the server rather than obtained by it.

Field F — TrustBoundaryNotes (2–5 bullets):
- The MCP Server executes git and related tools using the server process environment and mounted files, so any secrets present in process.env or mounted (SSH keys, .gitconfig) are used for egress without per-call restriction.
- There is no MCP-server-managed authentication flow (no OAuth/OIDC refresh, no token minting, no SDK credential selection); authority is inherited/delegated from host-provided secrets.
- Controls are limited to input validation and timeouts; there is no per-tool credential scoping or least-privilege enforcement inside the server—tools run with the full authority of provided credentials.
- Because credentials are passed through (env/file), multiple tools and operations may reuse the same global credentials unless deployment isolates them externally.

Final Conclusion:
Authorization exists.

Field A — EgressAuthorization (Primary): Exists

README instructs placing credentials.json and running generate_token.py to obtain token.json via browser consent.

Field C — InternalConstraints: Fully trusted by default
- The server code centrally loads and reuses a global credential (token.json / credentials.json) for tool executions without per-invocation authorization checks; the only programmatic constraint is the hard-coded SCOPES (calendar.readonly) and configured calendar IDs.

Field D — AuthorizationCategory (Open Taxonomy):
- OAuth InstalledAppFlow
- Local credential/token files
- SDK-mediated credentials (googleapiclient)

Field E — EvidenceSummary (2–5 bullets):
- main.py: authenticate_google_calendar() reads token.json / credentials.json, uses InstalledAppFlow.from_client_secrets_file(...) and flow.run_local_server(...), writes token.json, and returns creds.
- main.py: service = build("calendar", "v3", credentials=creds) — credentials are passed into outgoing API client.
- generate_token.py: same OAuth flow and token.json generation (README references running it to create token.json).
- calendar_settings.json & code: calendar IDs are loaded from local config and used without additional server-side auth checks.
- .gitignore lists credentials.json and token.json, confirming credentials flow through the project files.

Field F — TrustBoundaryNotes (2–5 bullets):
- Once token.json/credentials.json exist, any MCP tool invocation uses those credentials without per-request user consent or RBAC inside the server (global credential reuse).
- The server enforces only OAuth scope (calendar.readonly) as a capability constraint; no per-tool or per-user scoping is implemented.
- Credentials are local files (client secret + persisted tokens) and the server both obtains and stores tokens (it performs the OAuth flow and token management).
- Long-lived access is possible via refresh token usage (creds.refresh(Request())), meaning the server can continue egress calls over time until tokens are revoked.

Final Conclusion: Authorization exists.
